facts.fact: Substrate is the material laid on the bottom of an aquarium.
A main reason to add substrate is to give beneficial bacteria a surface to grow on, which supports biological filtration.
Substrate can release or absorb substances and so affect water quality. Calcium carbonate materials such as crushed coral raise carbonate hardness and buffer pH.
Many live plants root in the substrate. Some, such as Amazon swords and Vallisneria, take most of their food through their roots.
In planted tanks the substrate should stay loose enough for roots and be at least 5 cm (2 in) deep.
Cation exchange capacity (CEC) is a substrate's ability to hold nutrient ions where plant roots can reach them. A high CEC tells you nothing about how many nutrients the substrate actually contains.
In a home-made planted tank, the gravel layer is a place for plant roots, and it also works as a filter and as a place where fish spawn.
"lớp nền" is the term VnExpress uses for the substrate layer.
"nền thủy sinh" is the term the AquaSetup article uses for planted-tank substrate.
"Substrate (aquarium)" is the English term the encyclopedia article uses.
"Nền Cát" is the name the AquaZone shop uses for a sand substrate.
"Nền cát" is the name the M55 Aquarium shop uses, calling it the most traditional and easiest substrate to use in a planted tank.

"Phân nền" is the name Vietnamese shops and keepers use for the nutrient-rich granular soil itself (aqua soil), not for a fertiliser layer under it. Examples: "Phân nền ADA Amazonia", "Phân nền Gex Xanh", "Phân nền Akadama".
"cốt nền" is the name Wiki Cá Cảnh uses for an optional base layer laid under the soil to add nutrients and make the substrate last longer.
"cốt nền" and "phân nước" are what ShopThuySinh says to add to "Phân nền Akadama", because Akadama holds very few nutrients.
Phân nền comes as small round granules about 2–4 mm across, black or grey.
Phân nền releases nutrients slowly and lowers pH slightly, usually to just below 7.
Phân nền should be laid at least about 4 cm deep for planting.
Phân nền shifts easily, comes in few colours and can affect water quality, so research a product before buying.
Aqua soil is a clay-based, nutrient-rich substrate that lowers pH below 7 and softens water, which suits tropical fish and sensitive shrimp.
Soil was first made known by ADA as "Aqua Soil". It is mostly natural volcanic earth, rich in nutrients and trace elements, formed into granules and lightly burned.
Soil is often dark brown to black and comes in several grain sizes. Its granules hold their shape but are softer than gravel, which helps roots grow.
Soil is a cation exchanger. It lowers pH, general hardness (GH) and carbonate hardness (KH).
Soil's ability to exchange cations lasts only a couple of years. Hard tap water shortens this, and water changes with soft water make it last longer.
Soil suits soft-water shrimp such as the Red Bee (Caridina logemanni).
Some aqua soils release ammonia after they are added, which can cause ammonia spikes and algae in a new tank. Watch for ammonia spikes in a fresh tank.
Aquasoil can leach ammonia for the first 2–4 weeks, so cycle the tank before adding livestock.
Aqua soil does not suit live-bearers such as guppies, which need more minerals. Buce Plant suggests adding minerals at water changes or adding crushed coral.
Nutrient-rich substrate lowers pH and softens water, so using it in an African cichlid tank is a mistake.
With aqua soil, keep at least 1.5 in (about 4 cm) at the bottom for roots. Add root tabs after one or two years, as its nutrients run out.
"Phân nền ADA Amazonia": change about 30% of the water every day during the first week after setup, because of the soil's high Amazonia content.
"ADA Amazonia" is Japanese, made from 100% natural black soil in 2–4 mm granules. It helps balance pH and lower hardness. A 9 L bag (~8 kg) costs about 990,000đ.
"GEX Xanh" is a Japanese heat-treated natural black soil in 2–4 mm granules, pH 6.5–6.7, for plants with moderate nutrient needs. Lay it 5–6 cm deep, for example 4–5 kg for a 30x30x30 cm tank.
"GEX Đỏ" (GEX Shrimp Sand) is low in nutrients and has a pH of 6.0–6.5. It suits shrimp tanks and plants with low nutrient needs.
"Akadama" is a Japanese fired clay first made for bonsai. Wiki Cá Cảnh says it is very poor in nutrients, pH 6.5, and lists it at 35,000–55,000đ per kg.
"Phân nền S.Mekong II" is made in Vietnam, sold in 2 kg bags, with about 60–65% organic matter. Wiki Cá Cảnh says shrimp do well in it.
"Phân nền Aquafor (Thủy Mộc)" is a low-cost soil that clears after 12–18 hours of filtration and keeps pH at 6.5–7.2.
Wiki Cá Cảnh suggests replacing phân nền roughly every 3–5 years. Low-nutrient soils may need liquid fertiliser over time.
Home-mixed substrates (nền tự trộn) made from clay, worm castings and peat are not suited to beginners because they fail easily.
"Nền đất sét" (clay substrate) is rich in nutrients but can cloud the water if it is not treated properly.
In a layered substrate, the bottom nutrient layer such as ADA Power Sand combines pumice gravel with slow-release nutrients and beneficial bacteria.

Layered substrate, in order: 1–2 cm of coarse porous base (Power Sand, pumice or 2–5 mm lava rock granules); optional additives; 4–6 cm of aquasoil at the back sloping to 2–3 cm at the front; optional 3–5 mm cap of inert sand or fine gravel.
A thick cap of sand or gravel over the soil stops roots from reaching its nutrients.
A single soil layer typically loses its nutrients, compacts and forms anaerobic pockets within 6–12 months.
Black patches in the substrate or a hydrogen sulphide smell suggest anaerobic pockets.
Deep siphoning disturbs substrate layers and releases trapped gases.

VnExpress's home-made tank guide: lay the substrate 2–7 cm deep, with an optional 2–3 cm layer of "đất dinh dưỡng" (nutrient soil) underneath, then smooth it with a brush before adding rocks, roots and plants.
Sỏi (gravel) comes in many sizes, shapes and colours. AquaSetup mentions sỏi suối at 2–3 mm and larger pieces at 4–5 mm, and some kinds have sharp edges.
Sỏi is inert. It does not affect the water but supplies no minerals or nutrients, so planted tanks need liquid or tablet fertiliser.
Sỏi is cheap, widely sold and heavy enough to stay in place, and siphoning does not pull it up.
Food waste collects under sỏi, so it needs frequent siphoning. Sharp kinds can injure fish, and AquaSetup advises against large round glass pebbles.
Gravel, as Buce Plant writes it, ranges from small pebbles to river stones. It is inert, so it does not change water parameters.
Choose rounded gravel if you keep bottom-dwelling fish, because sharp edges can injure them.
Debris collects between gravel stones, so vacuum gravel during water changes.
Ordinary pet-store gravel grows stem, floating and rhizome plants if you dose a complete liquid fertiliser. Add root tabs for heavy root feeders.
Large river stones leave too much empty space for rooted plants to take hold.
Gravel is the most common freshwater substrate. It is usually quartz-based and should not be sharp. Fine gravel of 1–2 mm is often preferred in planted tanks.
VnExpress says sỏi of about 3 mm is popular for medium-sized tanks.
Cát (sand) is made of small rock particles, shell fragments and other impurities, in fine white, black or yellow grains. It does not affect the water and supplies no nutrients.
Cát suits bottom-dwelling fish with soft bellies, such as cá chuột.
Cát shifts easily, can be sucked into and clog the filter, packs too densely for roots and does not give beneficial bacteria enough oxygen.
White cát shows fish waste clearly, needs cleaning more often and can turn yellow over time.
Sand, as Buce Plant writes it, is fine and soft, and suits bottom feeders such as Corydoras (shown: Corydoras similis) and loaches.
Compacted sand can form anaerobic zones that convert nitrate back to ammonia. Use a thinner layer, keep bottom feeders that sift it, or stir it by hand.
Sand can be sucked into filters and pumps, so pour water in gently and take care not to siphon out sand.
Very fine sand compacts and makes it hard for roots to grow through. Coarse sand works better.
"Nền cát": rinse it thoroughly. M55 Aquarium suggests soaking it in salt water for about 24 hours to disinfect it, and laying it thicker at the back and thinner at the front.
"Nền Cát" holds water poorly and has too few nutrients for plants, so a planted sand tank needs more careful upkeep.
Sand is recommended for animals that bury themselves, such as river stingrays.
Soil and sand can be kept apart with hardscape, with dividers such as pond liner or PET sheets, or with moss pads on flat stones. Sloped soil often slides onto sand.
"Đá nham thạch" is volcanic rock. AquaSetup describes it as porous and light, yet heavy enough to sink, and says some pieces have sharp edges.
"Đá nham thạch" is usually inert, but some kinds release minerals or change pH and hardness. Its sharp edges can scratch bottom-dwelling fish.

"Sỏi Núi Lửa" is sold by Mayaqua under the English names Lava Gravel / Lava Rock. It is rock formed from cooled lava, porous and lighter than ordinary gravel, in reddish-brown, black or ash grey and in 3–5, 5–8 or 8–12 mm grains.

"Sỏi Núi Lửa": rinse thoroughly, soaking it 2–3 times and scrubbing gently to remove rock dust. Then spread a 1–2 cm base layer and cover it with aquasoil (such as ADA or Gex) or with sand or black gravel.
"Sỏi Núi Lửa" may raise pH slightly. Mayaqua advises testing before using it with tép ong (bee shrimp), and warns against using it alone as a planting substrate because it has no nutrients.
"Nham thạch trắng", also called đá lông vũ or đá bọt biển, is a white filter stone from Indonesia, 1–3 cm, sold at 30.000đ/1kg. ShopThuySinh says it can also be used as a base layer.
"Nham thạch trắng" floats when first soaked and sinks by itself later. ShopThuySinh says it does not affect hardness, pH or TDS.

Lava rock, as the English-language shop Gensou writes it (also volcanic rock or basalt scoria), forms when lava cools quickly and traps gas bubbles, leaving a porous, sponge-like stone. It is the same stone Vietnamese shops sell as đá nham thạch or sỏi núi lửa.

Lava rock is red (from iron oxide, burgundy to rusty orange) or black. Both colours have the same porosity and water effects, and it weighs about a third to a half as much as Seiryu or dragon stone of the same size.
Lava rock is pH neutral and does not significantly change pH or hardness. Its pores give nitrifying bacteria (Nitrosomonas, Nitrobacter) a large surface.
Preparing lava rock: rinse it under running water until the runoff is mostly clear, soak it 24 hours, then drain and rinse again. Optionally boil it 15 to 20 minutes, then do a vinegar test.
If a rock sold as lava rock fizzes in vinegar, it contains calcium carbonate (it may be limestone or tufa) and will raise pH. Genuine lava rock should not fizz.
Lava rock dust clouds the water if not cleaned off. Landscaping rock may carry fertilisers or pesticides. Avoid painted, dyed or sealed pieces.
File or sand down lava rock's sharp points. The barbels of bottom dwellers such as Corydoras and loaches are at risk, as are long-finned fish such as bettas, fancy guppies and angelfish.
Lava rock rubble can fill the lower layer to raise the back of the tank. Cover it with mesh or filter floss before adding soil.

"Xỉ than" (coal slag) is also sold as a substrate. Its iron oxide can tint the water orange and feed algae, its CaO can raise hardness, and poorly processed slag may contain heavy metals. Rinse it thoroughly.
"Peat moss" releases tannins that turn the water pale tea-coloured and lower pH. It suits blackwater tanks and breeding low-pH fish, but loose bits can drift and dirty the water.
Artificially dyed gravel or sand gives plant roots no nutrients, so it is a poor choice for a planted tank.
Assuming the most expensive substrate guarantees good results is a mistake.
Breeding tanks may use marbles so eggs fall out of the parents' reach. Quarantine tanks often have no substrate at all.
Mikrogeophagus ramirezi is pictured in a bare-bottom breeding or grow-out tank.
Tropica Substrate, sold in Vietnam as a cốt nền to lay under sand or aqua soil, comes as brown grains.
Tropica Substrate cốt nền has a grain size of 1-3 mm.
ADA Power Sand, a cốt nền, has grains that look like lava rock (đá nham thạch).
The Power Sand cốt nền is described as clean lava rock, with white pumice-like stone (nham thạch trắng) and brown lava rock (nham thạch nâu) mentioned as its materials.
Coal slag (xỉ than) sold for fish tanks has a muted, dark colour (màu sắc trầm).
Xỉ than pieces have uneven, irregular shapes.
Xỉ than is very porous with many tiny holes and is light in weight, and its pieces do not stick together or form clumps.
Xỉ than pieces come in random sizes. They are broken into moderately small pieces for filter use, while larger pieces are used to anchor plants. No grain size in mm is given.
Hugo Kamishi Akadama Small Grain is made of porous volcanic clay particles 1-4 mm in size.
Premium Ibaraki akadama forms hard, porous granules of a clay-like mineral.
Akadama is sold in grades: Shohin (under 1/16 inch), Small (1/16 to 1/4 inch) and Medium (1/4 to 1/2 inch).
Akadama darkens when it is moist.
Softer grades of akadama can break down into smaller particles.
Ibaraki akadama sold for aquariums is a hard-grade Japanese clay soil with a natural clay texture and earthy colour. It should be rinsed to remove fine dust before use.
Peat moss is a brown fibrous material.
Peat moss is sold for aquarium use as compressed sphagnum peat moss pellets. Peat pucks sold for sprouting garden seeds can also go in a filter or sump.
Dried sphagnum moss can be light brown or white.
Aquarium peat is sold as granules (also called pellets) and as fibrous peat. Granules are easier to keep in filter media bags and less messy.
Fibrous peat releases tannins faster than granules but can clog filter intakes if not bagged.
Fluval Aquatic Peat Granules are sold in 500 g packs as chemical filter media for canister filters.
